name: Predictive Analytics of Air Alerts in the Russian-Ukrainian War (Pavlyshenko & Pavlyshenko, arXiv:2411.14625)
year: 2024 (v1 submitted 21 Nov 2024; no later version found as of 2026-10-17)
authors: Demian Pavlyshenko, Bohdan Pavlyshenko (affiliations not stated in the paper; B. Pavlyshenko is associated with Ivan Franko National University of Lviv [uncertain])
popularity: Low; citation count not retrieved (Semantic Scholar API rate-limited); a few secondary summaries exist (themoonlight.io review, chatpaper) [uncertain]
peer_review_status: preprint (arXiv cs.LG / cs.AI / cs.CY, no journal ref)
target_type: Mixed state/persistence target, effectively a STATE target: label = 1 if the oblast is under alert 5 (or 15) minutes ahead, i.e. an alert starts within the window when none is active, OR an ongoing alert lasts at least 5 more minutes. Rows already under alert are included, so the label is dominated by persistence of the current state. Test positive rates (5-min horizon): Lviv 1.4%, Vinnytsia 9.1%, Kyiv oblast 19.3%, Kharkiv 55.2%. These are shares of time under alert, not onset rates.
target_definition: Binary per-minute label per region: 'alert will be in the region within the next 5 minutes' (appendix: 15 minutes). The paper describes it in prose. If no alert is active, the label is 1 if an alert starts in the window. If an alert is active, the label is 1 if it lasts at least the horizon. The label is 0 if no alert starts or the alert ends within the window. H = 5 min (main) and 15 min (appendix). No target-construction code is published, and the exact shift/lag indexing is unspecified.
spatial_unit: oblast. Separate models for 4 oblasts: Lvivska, Vinnytska, Kyivska, Kharkivska. Features use all oblasts plus Kyiv City.
at_risk_masking: No. Test support is 184,316 minute rows per region, which equals every minute from 2024-07-01 to 2024-11-06 (128 days x 1440). Minutes already under alert are therefore kept in both training and scoring. Kharkiv has 101,748 positive test minutes out of 184,316, so most 'positives' are continuation of an active alert. This is the key reason the reported accuracy/AUC are inflated relative to an onset task.
data_sources: Vadym Klymenko (Vadimkin) 'ukrainian-air-raid-sirens-dataset' on GitHub, resampled to a 1-minute time series from 2022-03-25 to 2024-11-06. No other sources (no ISW, Telegram, weather, launch counts) are used in the model. The intro mentions the authors' earlier Telegram/NLP alert-prediction channel, but it is not used here.
data_source_variant: Which file (official_data vs volunteer_data) is not stated [uncertain]. Oblast-level region names appear in the features ('Lvivska oblast', 'Kyiv City', ..., 'Luhanska oblast'). There is no mention of raion/hromada alerts or of building an admin-level union, so they probably used oblast-level rows only, or used the dataset's oblast column without discussion [uncertain]. The snapshot is the dataset as of about 2024-11-06. The data predates the 2025 raion/hromada reform and the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform.
preprocessing: Each region is converted to a binary 1-minute series (1 = alert active). They also build a cumulative 'alert time' feature equal to the running duration of the current alert (0 when there is none), and calendar features. No deduplication, gap detection, admin-level union, standing-alert handling or duration-artefact handling is described. Luhansk is noted to have short coverage but is kept as a feature, where it gets zero importance.
known_label_artefacts: None of the known artefacts are discussed. (1) Duplicates: not mentioned. Duplicates would not change a binary 'active' series much, but they matter for onset counts. (2) Exactly-30-minute/naive end times: not mentioned. (3) Standing alerts (multi-month hromada alerts): not mentioned. They are less relevant to a 2022-2024 oblast-level series, but any raion-level rows would inflate the 'active' state. (4) Recording gaps: not mentioned. Gaps would be silently encoded as 'no alert'. (5) Luhansk permanent alert: kept as a feature, not excluded. (6) Paper-level artefacts: Fig. 20-21 (Kharkiv 5-min importance/ROC) reuse the Kyivska image files, so the Kharkiv 5-min ROC is not actually shown. Fig. 30's caption is wrong.
model_family: Random Forest (scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier, n_estimators=500, random_state=15, other hyperparameters default). One model per target region. Hard-threshold predictions (predict) give accuracy/classification report. predict_proba gives ROC. No tuning and no other model families are compared.
features: (a) Binary alert-active features for all oblasts plus Kyiv City at the forecast time, described as 'lagged values'. The number of lags and the lag step are not specified, and the importance plots show one feature per region, suggesting one lag. The target region's OWN current state is included and is the top feature for Lviv (about 0.20 importance). Neighbours follow (Volynska 0.14, Ivano-Frankivska 0.13, Zakarpatska, Ternopilska, Rivnenska). (b) Cumulative current-alert duration ('alert time'/'f' features). (c) Calendar: hour, weekday, month. (d) 'ndays' = days since dataset start, a trend/time-index feature that can encode regime but extrapolates poorly. No external features.
external_feature_timing: Not applicable. No external features (ISW, Telegram, weather, launch counts) are used.
ablation_design: None. There is no feature ablation, and the only interpretability evidence is RF impurity feature importances. The claims that neighbouring regions and seasonality matter rest on impurity importance only (which is biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features).
split_scheme: Single chronological hold-out: train = all minutes before 2024-07-01 (from 2022-03-25), test = 2024-07-01 to 2024-11-06. No validation set, no walk-forward, no refits, no purge at the cut-off. With a 5-min horizon the leak across the boundary is negligible.
metrics: Accuracy, sklearn classification report (precision/recall/F1 per class, macro/weighted averages), confusion matrix, ROC-AUC. No Brier, log loss, BSS or PR-AUC.
unit_of_metric: Per-region (within-oblast) metrics. Each oblast's model is scored separately on its own minute rows. No pooled metric.
baseline_strength: No baselines at all: no persistence, climatology or recent rate. A raw persistence baseline ('state at t+5 = state at t') would likely achieve similar accuracy/AUC on this state target, because alerts last tens of minutes to hours and only about 1 in N minute transitions changes state [uncertain: not computed in the paper]. Skill versus the strongest baseline is therefore unknown.
calibration: Not assessed. No reliability plot or calibration method. RF predict_proba is used only for ROC.
calibration_under_drift: Not assessed. The paper notes that 'ndays' is important for some regions, i.e. the alert pattern shifts over time. The Kyiv oblast alert-time plot shows much longer alerts from August 2024 (inside the test period), which is a visible base-rate shift between train and test. It is not quantified and there is no recalibration.
uncertainty_of_gain: None. No CIs, bootstrap or significance tests. Single seed, single split.
regime_coverage: Covers 2022-03 to 2024-11 only. The test window (Jul-Nov 2024) includes the summer/autumn-2024 increase in long drone alerts. It predates the Jan-2025 drone surge, the 2025 raion/hromada reform (Dec-2025) and the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform, so none of these shifts is covered.
leakage_handling: Chronological split with train strictly before 2024-07-01. Features are described as current/lagged values, so no obvious look-ahead in the features. However: (1) no truncation test or leakage audit; (2) the cumulative 'alert time' feature and the binary state are computed from the active/inactive series, which is causal only if alert ends are known in real time (true for live alerts, so acceptable); (3) target-construction code is not published, so whether the label window aligns exactly with the feature time cannot be verified [uncertain]; (4) no purge at the cut-off (immaterial for H = 5-15 min); (5) 'ndays' is causal but is a time index that is out of range in the test set; (6) the main validity problem is not leakage but the target design. Including in-alert minutes makes 'predicting' an active alert trivial from the region's own current state.
test_window_hygiene: Single test split. No validation set, so any choices (horizon, n_estimators = 500, feature set) could only have been made by looking at the test set or not at all. No pre-registration. Model trained once per region with fixed hyperparameters.
headline_results: 5-minute horizon, test 2024-07-01 to 2024-11-06, 184,316 minutes per region (read from classification-report and ROC screenshots in the paper's figures). Lviv: accuracy 0.99, positive-class precision 0.81 / recall 0.61 / F1 0.70, support 2,649 positives, ROC-AUC 0.96. Vinnytsia: accuracy 0.97, P 0.93 / R 0.72 / F1 0.81, 16,849 positives, ROC-AUC 0.98. Kyiv oblast: accuracy 0.93, P 0.96 / R 0.69 / F1 0.80, 35,573 positives, ROC-AUC 0.99. Kharkiv: accuracy 0.86, P 0.96 / R 0.78 / F1 0.86, 101,748 positives (55%). The Kharkiv 5-min ROC figure is a duplicate of Kyiv's. The Kharkiv 15-min ROC-AUC is 0.87. Other 15-min results are in the appendix and were not all transcribed [uncertain]. None of these numbers are compared to any baseline. Because they are scored on a state target that includes in-alert minutes, they mostly reflect persistence and are NOT comparable to an onset-forecast AUC. The surprisingly low recall (0.61-0.78) at a 5-minute horizon suggests the RF misses many alert minutes, plausibly the onset minutes and the first minutes of alerts [uncertain].
code_available: Partial. Only the train/validate function (RandomForest fit, classification report, ROC plot) is printed in Appendix A.2. There is no repository, no target/feature-construction code and no data snapshot. The paper is licensed CC BY 4.0 on arXiv. The underlying dataset is public on GitHub (Vadimkin).
takeaways_for_project: (1) This is the only academic paper found on forecasting UA alerts, and it uses a STATE target with no at-risk masking. It is the anti-example motivating our onset target plus mask ('rows already under alert are excluded', CLAUDE.md Target; leakage test asserts the mask). Its high AUCs (0.96-0.99) must not be cited as a benchmark for our onset AUC. (2) No baselines: our D-021 requirement (BSS vs rolling recent rate, plus climatology, raw and calibrated persistence) directly addresses this gap. When citing this paper we should note that persistence likely matches it. (3) The finding that neighbouring regions dominate (Lviv <- Volyn, Ivano-Frankivsk, Zakarpattia, Ternopil, Rivne) supports our neighbors_active_at_t and national_active_count_at_t features (D-017 border table in src/regions.py). Under an onset target, the useful signal is neighbours turning on while the target is still off. (4) Their 'ndays' trend feature and visibly longer alerts in the test period (Aug-Nov 2024) illustrate drift. We prefer the rolling recent-rate baseline and calibration-in-the-large checks (D-015/D-021) over a raw time index, which extrapolates out of range. (5) They do no deduplication, gap masking, standing-alert handling or admin-level union, which we do (dedup count, D-013 gap mask, D-020 causal 24h cap, union of levels). This is a methodological contrast for the README's related-work section. (6) Their minute resolution and 5-15 min horizon are a different use case (imminence) from our hourly H = 1. Our results are not comparable in scale either.
best_practices: Adopt: chronological split by date rather than random rows; per-region evaluation; spatial-neighbour features; simple, interpretable models; publishing the training function. Anti-patterns to avoid: (a) a state target that includes in-alert rows, which inflates accuracy/AUC through persistence; (b) accuracy on heavily imbalanced data (Lviv 98.6% negatives gives 0.99 'accuracy'); (c) no naive baselines; (d) no probabilistic metrics (Brier/BSS, PR-AUC) and no calibration/reliability plots; (e) a single split with no validation set, so hyperparameters cannot be selected without test peeking; (f) impurity-based feature importance as the sole evidence of feature value, without ablation on the same sample; (g) an unbounded time-index feature (ndays) that the model must extrapolate in the test set; (h) no data-quality handling (duplicates, gaps, permanent alerts like Luhansk kept as features); (i) no uncertainty on results (single seed, no bootstrap); (j) unpublished label-construction code, so the horizon alignment cannot be audited; mislabeled/duplicated figures.
